# 13. Interface and accessibility

A roguelike's player meets its rules only through the screen, the keys and the message log. That makes the interface the place where a deep game is either opened up or shut off: whether a newcomer can tell a small dragon from a big one, whether a veteran can move as fast as they think, whether a blind player can play at all. This chapter covers commands and input devices, the cost of options, speed and automation, previews and tooltips, the meaning carried by messages and labels, ways of making large simulations legible, the choice between letters, tiles and symbols, the mechanics of putting them on a screen, and accessibility for blind players, children, parents, newcomers and different minds.

The talks share a through-line. A game's depth should live in its systems, not in the effort it takes to operate them, and the people best placed to tell you where that effort lies are the players you are not. Several speakers learned this from playtests that went badly or from communities whose praise turned out not to speak for everyone. The genre's text heritage turns out to be an advantage here as well as a burden: a game that already describes its world in words is unusually close to being playable without sight.

## In brief

- Interface work is a large part of a roguelike's design, not polish applied at the end: Subset Games spends half or more of its development time on UX, and Angband made itself approachable without making itself easier ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 7:18](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=438); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 11:28](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=688)).
- Do not let veterans alone judge your interface: Thomas Biskup found that twenty years of praise for ADOM's UI from power users did not survive contact with Steam, Santiago Zapata argues that competition has raised the bar, and Josh Ge urges importing the conveniences of non-roguelike games ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 7:24](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=444); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 10:51](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=651); [Santiago Zapata 2017, 18:21](https://youtu.be/wwc7pZqs9UA?t=1101); [Josh Ge 2016, 21:21](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1281)).
- Keep the depth in the game logic and the command set small, design the simple interface first and add power-user tools afterwards, and make every action reachable without memorised keys ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:34](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=934); [Thomas Biskup 2019, 12:59](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=779); [Thomas Biskup 2017, 27:09](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1629); [Josh Ge 2016, 20:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1214)).
- Make movement the main verb and let context decide what a move does, as bump-to-attack, step-on stairs and single-button designs independently show ([slashie 2026, 9:08:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32933); [George Moromisato 2016, 17:17](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1037); [Brian Walker 2018, 18:28](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1108)).
- Never make the player wait on animation, and automate decisions that have only one right answer ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 11:16](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=676); [Jeremiah Reid 2021, 18:59](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1139); [Josh Ge 2016, 22:56](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1376); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 13:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=807); [bhauth 2020, 3:43](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=223)).
- Show outcomes before the player commits, and get previews cheaply and exactly by running the real game code on a copy of the game state, which you must design for from the start ([Brian Cronin 2021, 7:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=426); [Brian Cronin 2024, 27:04](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1624); [Danny Day 2018, 15:08](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=908)).
- For deep simulations, give players instruments for sense-making, such as filters, chronicles, journals and summaries of hidden state, rather than a raw feed of events ([Max Kreminski 2019, 11:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=701); [Jasmine Otto 2021, 2:45](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=165); [Jonathan Lessard 2023, 4:32](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=272); [Cat Manning 2020, 19:11](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1151)).
- Treat ASCII versus tiles as a trade-off between telling symbols apart and knowing what they mean, and if you add tiles, re-encode every signal the glyphs carried ([Joel Ryan 2022, 13:57](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=837); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 4:36](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=276); [Joel Ryan 2022, 8:56](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=536)).
- A text-based roguelike is unusually close to playable by blind players, but only testing with visually impaired players shows what they need ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 12:09](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=729); [Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)).
- Find the players you are not with cheap simulations and by listening for recurring newcomer questions: unreadable fonts for pre-literate children, sitting further back for older eyes, random button-mashing on menus ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 21:11](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1271); [Michael Langford 2021, 10:24](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=624); [Michael Langford 2021, 10:58](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=658); [Michael Langford 2021, 9:29](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=569)).

## The interface is the design: why roguelike UI decides who can play

### Presentation failures look like design failures

A roguelike's rules can be sound and still lose the player, because the player meets the rules only through the screen. Two very different teams make the same point. Erik Osheim and Robert Au describe Angband's ergonomic changes as an attempt to make the game approachable and comfortable for new players without making it any easier. The first of them were on-screen monster and item lists: before them, you could not easily tell whether the detected red `d` five tiles away was a small dragon or a big one, and an item list helps you set goals once objects are detected ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 11:28](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=688)). Nothing about the game's difficulty changed; what changed was whether you could see the information the game already had.

Justin Ma and Matthew Davis of Subset Games tell the same story at larger scale. Early playtests of Into the Breach were painful because players did not understand what to expect or what to do. Their diagnosis was that the design was fine and the presentation was not; fixes such as animated tooltips made a massive difference, and the biggest lesson was how little people understood of what the developers thought was clear. They estimate that half or more of the development time on their games goes to user experience (UX) ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 7:18](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=438)).

> It wasn't a case of the design being bad, it was a case of the presentation being problematic. — [Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 7:18](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=438)

If you take one thing from this section, take that budget figure. UX is not a coat of polish applied once the systems are finished; on Subset's games it is, by their estimate, half or more of the work.

### The community bubble

The sharpest warning comes from Thomas Biskup, whose ADOM had nearly twenty years of feedback calling its interface slick and optimised. When the game reached Steam, the reaction was that it was unplayable. Biskup blames himself for getting caught in the community bubble, which fed decisions that were not good for the game, and draws a blunt conclusion: roguelike communities, however great, are probably the biggest obstacle to mainstream-friendly interfaces ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 7:24](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=444)). The reason is who those communities are. They are dominated by power users, whom he likens to Olympic athletes: they feel every inefficiency, demand optimised tools, endless options and ever more detail, and they argue so well and so confidently that their feedback feels universally valid when it is not ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 10:51](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=651)). What works for them is not what works for casual or mainstream players.

Biskup is candid about the cost in his own game. He names ADOM's accessibility, with too many hard-to-use commands and a UI cobbled onto a decades-old game, as one of its biggest sins and something very hard to change later ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 2:34](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=154)). A year earlier he had already listed making ADOM less hard for newcomers who do not know how roguelikes work as the first priority for the game's future, with the graphical interface as the place to do it ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 6:37](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=397)).

### The bar has risen

Several designers who otherwise have little in common converge on the view that the genre can no longer afford its old interfaces. Santiago Zapata argues that roguelikes reaching a wider audience cannot rely on unusable interfaces or mechanics nobody understands, because competition has raised the bar, and sees this as healthy for the genre ([Santiago Zapata 2017, 18:21](https://youtu.be/wwc7pZqs9UA?t=1101)). Slashie, the handle under which Zapata gave a 2026 talk on two decades of his games, calls his longest-running design question how far a traditional roguelike's entry barrier can be lowered, now that players have largely moved to phones, without losing its essence ([slashie 2026, 9:07:12](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32832)). Josh Ge points to Cogmind's player statistics, which show heavy use of the mouse and of tiles: documentation, a tutorial, full mouse support and a tileset greatly widen the audience, though a first game can still be ASCII and keyboard-only, and some of these features need to be in the design from the beginning ([Josh Ge 2018, 26:31](https://youtu.be/jviNpRGuCIU?t=1591)). His prescription is to import the standard conveniences of non-roguelike games, such as clicking a stat to learn what it does, as long as the result stays a roguelike ([Josh Ge 2016, 21:21](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1281)). Casey Yano makes the parallel case for digital card games: a computer can explain rules in context, shuffle for you, and clarify rules by enforcing them in code, so the digital version should never feel like a sad substitute for the physical one ([Casey Yano 2022, 5:17](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=317)).

### Counterweights

Three things pull against simply modernising. First, conventions are sticky. Tabitha Sable shows that the software people are used to shapes what they want next, so old hardware limits persist for decades: modern editors still offer vi key bindings descended from a terminal without arrow keys ([Tabitha Sable 2020, 25:02](https://youtu.be/6ohPU0sECFE?t=1502)). Biskup accepted this for ADOM's existing players, promising the "old guard" no more groundbreaking overhauls that force them to unlearn what they had learned, while still improving accessibility ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 6:51](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=411)). Changing an interface has a cost for the people already fluent in it.

Second, polish is not the same as speed. John Bond calls polish the luck variable because it affects everything: players accept Persona 5's slow menus because they are so well polished ([John Bond 2024, 9:04](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=544)). Jeremiah Reid argues that even strategy and resource-management games benefit from juice in buttons and unlocks, since no one can argue their game has enough polish ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 28:49](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1729)). Polish buys tolerance, but it does not excuse an interface that wastes the player's time; the section on speed below sets limits on it.

Third, there is no clean answer. Todd Furmanski says anyone who claims UI is easy is lying: controllers make mundane actions hard to teach, a phone is a flat glass surface, and both too much interface and none at all can be bad. It is a matter of picking your poison ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 17:04](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=1024)).

**In practice.** Budget for UX from the first day, and expect it to be a large share of the work ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 7:18](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=438)). Distrust feedback that comes only from veterans, however articulate ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 10:51](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=651)). Separate "harder to operate" from "harder to win" and remove the first without touching the second ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 11:28](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=688)). And keep Ma and Davis's open question in view: what would a classic roguelike with the best, clearest UI look like? They think it a hard but worthwhile goal; the interviewer recalled user-testing NetHack with students who had never played and finding that cheat sheets were never enough ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 19:56](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1196)).

## Simple surface, deep game: commands, options and detail levels

### Depth in the logic, not in the keys

The genre's strength is intricate mechanics that combine. Biskup's rule is to keep that depth in the game logic and hide it from the interface: a cool action that needs ten key presses will be used by perhaps one player in a thousand, so do not clutter the UI or over-explain how to do the clever things ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:34](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=934)).

> Hide the complexity on the UI side. Have it in the game logic, that's wonderful, but not in the user interface. — [Thomas Biskup 2019, 15:34](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=934)

His numbers for Ultimate ADOM make the argument concrete. ADOM has more than 100 keyboard commands, configuration spread over several files, and mouse support that took twenty years. Ultimate ADOM targets seven keys (WASD, E, F and space), because about 90% of players die within roughly 3,000 turns and never need the power commands; the interface has to be understandable without explanation for those short-lived players, which 100 commands make impossible ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 12:59](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=779)). The order of work matters as much as the count. Ultimate ADOM is designed mobile-first and controller-first, with power-user tools added afterwards, because reducing an already complex interface to simplicity, as ADOM's team had to, is a constant struggle ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 27:09](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1629)). Start simple and add speed for experts; do not start complex and try to subtract.

### Contextual action through movement

The strongest convergence in this section is on one idea: make movement the main verb and let the situation decide what a move means. Independent designers arrived at it, or at the related aim of cutting menus and prompts, from different directions.

- **Movement plus one button.** Slashie traces a line from CastlevaniaRL through a game where skills were first triggered by movement to Rodney and his later Steam roguelike: streamline the UI and the systems so that depth comes from simple commands and movement, drop redundant or historical commands, and trigger actions by moving or using the space around you instead of through menus ([slashie 2026, 9:08:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32933)). In Rodney, as Zapata described it in 2016, you have movement and a single action button, and a wall-jump skill fires when you run into a wall ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 17:20](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1040)).
- **Bump as the core verb, rare verbs on demand.** George Moromisato explains how NetHack keeps a huge verb set without swamping newcomers: moving, and attacking by bumping, is the key command, and rarer verbs sit in secondary menus. A newcomer just moves and attacks until a closed door or a need to search teaches a new verb; finding a lamp prompts them to look up whether lamps can be rubbed. Diablo takes the other route of a single default click action, so no manual is needed ([George Moromisato 2016, 17:17](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1037)).
- **Place things so stepping on them means using them.** Brian Walker's Brogue puts stairs in dead-end alcoves, walled on all sides but one, where the open side is not a choke point or hallway, so there is no other reason to enter the tile and stepping onto it can mean using the stairs, with no separate command ([Brian Walker 2018, 18:28](https://youtu.be/Uo9-IcHhq_w?t=1108)).
- **Items that need no further input.** Michael Brough points out that Rogue's scroll of teleportation sends you somewhere random rather than somewhere chosen, consistent with Rogue's choice that item effects need no further input after activation; a chosen destination would need another prompt ([Michael Brough 2021, 20:10](https://youtu.be/X4be22WoVgg?t=1210)).
- **No menu at all.** Spencer Egart's procedural ritual spells refuse a menu or targeting popup altogether: everything the effect needs, such as its target or element, must be specified by the ritual's own actions. That puts a burden on the generator, which has to know each effect's requirements and make sure some step satisfies them, for example a step that names the target ([Spencer Egart 2019, 5:28](https://youtu.be/q4Tf0vf2kiI?t=328)).
- **Borrow controls players already know.** Nick Bush's Word Processor starts from the observation that Rogue was shaped by the Unix terminal and asks what a roguelike would be if its creator had only used a word processor. His first takeaway is to ask which mechanics are already intuitive for players on a given platform, and to build from those ([Nick Bush 2026, 42:34](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=2554)).

### Mouse, touch and the keys you never find

The keyboard may not be the device most of your players use. Cogmind uses every key and about 300 commands, yet Ge's player data shows keyboard users are a minority; among movement inputs the numpad is most common and vi-keys least. His advice is to make every action reachable by mouse first, add drag-and-drop inventory, and let players move to the faster keyboard gradually ([Josh Ge 2016, 20:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1214)). Zapata reached the same conclusion for phones: ports of desktop roguelikes with many commands were very hard to play on touch screens, so a mobile roguelike has to be designed for touch from the start ([Santiago Zapata 2016, 18:52](https://youtu.be/TMxzVy7-VYQ?t=1132)).

Memorised shortcuts fail casual players silently. Biskup tells of an experienced gamer, an ADOM fan, who spent years not knowing he could drink potions, because `d` drops and drink is Shift-D; he assumed potions were only for selling. A casual player who tries something and fails gives up on the concept ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 11:52](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=712)). Some of these conventions are not design at all: the `hjkl` movement keys of vi and roguelikes come from the ADM-3A terminal, whose keyboard had no arrow keys but printed arrows on h, j, k and l ([Tabitha Sable 2020, 13:43](https://youtu.be/6ohPU0sECFE?t=823)). A hardware accident of one early terminal is not a reason to make it your only scheme.

### Options cost everyone

Options look free to the person who asked for them. Biskup's rule is that every visible option costs every player the effort of understanding it, and a page of 60 options makes a game look forbidding. A well-designed game with good defaults does not need a thousand options; Ultimate ADOM starts with essentials only (sound, resolution, key customisation) in a structured menu where players expect it ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 14:04](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=844)).

The alternative to options is designed layers of detail. Ultimate ADOM offers detail levels, from bars only, through some numbers, to full modifiers and engine internals for power users. Biskup stresses that this has to be planned from the beginning; ADOM has one detail level baked into its DNA and retrofitting more would mean rewriting too much ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 21:25](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1285)). A test result shows why it matters: more than half of the role-players tested could not read dice notation like 4d3+2 and silently ignored it. A range like 6-14 loses the distribution that 4d3+2 conveys, but casual players do not care, and the simplest display might be a single strength number ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 17:28](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1048)). So the simpler mode spells out abbreviations like DV and PV and shows a battle axe as 3 to 8 damage, keeping dice notation for experts; Biskup admits there is still too much statistics on screen ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 32:18](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=1938)).

Three supporting techniques make layers like these cheaper:

- **Small numbers.** Benjamin Berman's rule for accessible card combat is to put everything you need on the card: short decks, small-number arithmetic, few keywords, and no inflated values with extra zeroes ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 12:34](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=754)).
- **Explanations generated from data.** Because Ultimate ADOM models maps, items, monsters, races and quests as data in an entity-component system (ECS), the game can introspect any definition and generate a readable tooltip, so the Archer can be shown as "+1 strength, +4 toughness", and hovering over anything shows its statistics and modifiers. In hard-coded ADOM every explanation was written by hand ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 9:32](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=572)).
- **Per-platform rules.** Biskup imagines a mobile variant of Ultimate ADOM that drops item identification or status effects where they would be too fiddly, on the same engine ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 16:30](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=990)).

Density is not automatically the enemy. bhauth argues that aesthetics and information density are not directly in conflict, only that doing both is harder than doing one; Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (DCSS) chooses dense numbers over spectacle ([bhauth 2020, 19:02](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=1142)). What matters is whether the player can choose how much of that density to see.

### Multiplayer reaches the same rules

Tyriq Plummer arrived at the same constraints for a different reason: in a multiplayer roguelike, other players are waiting for your turn. HVNTRS is deterministic with no dice, has no menus, puts every action within two button presses, and hides no information, which also makes it welcoming to newcomers ([Tyriq Plummer 2020, 14:43](https://youtu.be/neuJCYmbAG8?t=883)). In Scrubbin' Trubble his team limited the decision space with small inventories, distinct enemies and a clearly readable state, avoiding menu diving and colour-swap enemy variants whose differences must be memorised, so players could glance at the board and act ([Tyriq Plummer 2025, 5:26](https://youtu.be/UNBAoc0TJSs?t=326)). When designers solving for speed and designers solving for newcomers converge on the same rules, the rules are probably sound.

**In practice.**

- One core verb, usually movement, with bump and step-on triggers for the common actions ([slashie 2026, 9:08:53](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32933); [George Moromisato 2016, 17:17](https://youtu.be/QBZkvtGucBU?t=1037)).
- Every action reachable by mouse or touch; the keyboard as an accelerator, not a requirement ([Josh Ge 2016, 20:14](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1214)).
- Few visible options with good defaults ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 14:04](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=844)).
- Detail levels designed in from the start, with simple numbers at the bottom and the full model at the top ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 21:25](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=1285)).

## Respecting the player's time: speed, automation and tedium

### Never make the player wait on the presentation

Jeremiah Reid has one rule for animation in a traditional roguelike that he says must be followed: never block the player from acting as fast as they want. Mashing a key to fly across the map is a staple of the genre, and critics associate juice with slow press-wait-press play, citing Dungeons of Dredmor ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 11:16](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=676)). His technique: apply every keypress immediately and speed up the animations still pending. With anticipation delays, pressing right twice originally moved the player only once; Reid now processes every input and doubles the speed of each outstanding animation, so a dozen tiles cross in about twice the time of a single move ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 18:59](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1139)).

Thomas Robertson marks the exception. Big super attacks are a big deal and have always stopped everything, so input can simply be inhibited while the queue of effects is non-empty, with skip or fast-forward offered so the player is not held up ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 4:00](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=240)). The two positions fit together: ordinary moves must never wait on visuals, and a rare spectacle may pause play if the player can cut it short.

Latency in the systems behind the screen does the same damage. Colin Liotta describes the roguelike puzzle in the 2017 MIT Mystery Hunt, whose server simulated each turn; under a hundred teams' load every move took about ten seconds, and with no undo, an accidental bump into an enemy meant an agonising restart ([Colin Liotta 2018, 5:02](https://youtu.be/5VsM8bOywIY?t=302)).

### Automate the no-brainers

The second convergence is on automating decisions that have only one right answer. Ge's example from Cogmind is a single key that swaps a damaged part for a less damaged one of the same type, picking up the better part, attaching it, and dropping or storing the old one; inventory sorting and stat comparison bars do the same job elsewhere. He stresses that plenty of real decisions remain ([Josh Ge 2016, 22:56](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1376)). Cogmind also labels robots, parts and objects automatically as they come into view, because nobody should need a look command to identify the debris after an explosion; the labels are optional and their duration configurable ([Josh Ge 2016, 21:39](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1299)). Angband's one-keystroke "fire at nearest monster" replaced a target-cursor-fire sequence and made missile attacks roughly as easy as bumping to melee, with less strain on the hands ([Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 13:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=807)).

DCSS shows where automation comes from in a community game. bhauth explains that many common activities, auto-explore among them, have automation because whenever players got annoyed by something repetitive, someone submitted a fix; auto-explore can even run instantly, helping real-time speedrunners average 20 moves a second, while a careful win-streak player would reveal as few tiles as possible ([bhauth 2020, 3:43](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=223)). In a first-person open world the same problem appears as walking: Furmanski notes that one walking speed is boring over long distances and awkward near objects, so Forska lets you click a far island or a nearby tree's shadow and be placed there ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 7:37](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=457)).

The cost of not thinking about this is shown by the game that preceded Dwarf Fortress. Zach and Tarn Adams's Mutant Miner became an interminable turn-based slog once it had several miners, mostly clicking repeatedly with nothing to fight, because, in their words, they had not thought about the interface at all ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 13:33](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=813)).

### When effort is the point

Not everyone wants friction removed. Zeno Rogue notes that auto-travel is controversial in traditional roguelikes, and HyperRogue omits it: navigating hyperbolic space is a challenge in its own right ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 18:02](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1082)). When the host, Alexei, said that memorising NetHack's whole-keyboard commands made playing feel wizard-like, Martin Pichlmair agreed that getting the body to do the work brings the player closer to the game ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 30:10](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1810)). Yong Zhen Zhou calls simplifying demanding inputs a mixed bag: it improves accessibility, but the motions give a game energy, act as a limiter and reward practice ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 16:23](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=983)). And some games make menu time a deliberate risk: Plummer notes that Vagante and Cave Blazers do not pause while the inventory is open, so swapping gear or hunting for a healing item mid-fight is dangerous ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 23:46](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1426)).

The choice depends on whether the effort is the game. If navigating, executing or managing under pressure is what you want the player to master, keep it, as HyperRogue and Vagante do ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 18:02](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1082); [Tyriq Plummer 2017, 23:46](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1426)). If it is a toll the player pays to reach the next decision, automate it, and keep the automation optional, as Cogmind does with its labels ([Josh Ge 2016, 21:39](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1299)).

**In practice.** Apply input immediately and let visuals catch up ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 18:59](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=1139)). Let rare spectacles pause play only if they can be skipped ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 4:00](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=240)). Automate decisions with one right answer ([Josh Ge 2016, 22:56](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1376)). Ask of each manual action whether its effort is part of the fun.

## Making consequences visible: previews, tooltips and threat display

### Interface design is directing attention

Joseph Hewitt frames UI with a magician's principle: just as a card trick works by directing the viewer's attention to one card, a game has to direct the player's attention deliberately to what they need to know and do. When players miss a required mechanic, it is because the designer failed to draw their attention to it ([Joseph Hewitt 2024, 6:27](https://youtu.be/dCWWId16VAo?t=387)). Everything in this section is a technique for aiming attention at consequences before they happen.

### Show the outcome before the commitment

Several talks converge on previews: let the player see what an action will do before they commit to it. Brian Cronin says Monster Train needed damage previews to ship. With many units, statuses and artifacts on the board, resolution was confusing; hovering a card now shows a red X on every unit that will die, updating if another spell changes the equation, and players really enjoy it ([Brian Cronin 2021, 7:06](https://youtu.be/qO3CIpP62Q0?t=426)). Dylan White shows Rift Wizard displaying every tile that is unsafe from enemy ranged attacks, so you can see which cultists can hit you and position accordingly ([Dylan White 2020, 23:48](https://youtu.be/VVRomN99Ygw?t=1428)).

The hard part is implementation, and two talks give the same answer from opposite sides. Cronin's black box sim makes previews easy: copy the world state, run the command on the copy, and read the resulting state changes to show, say, total damage. Because the preview runs the normal game code, it is accurate for every effect, including passive relic-style effects. Undo works the same way, by saving the world state at the start of a turn and copying it back, and custom world states also make automated tests possible ([Brian Cronin 2024, 27:04](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1624)). Danny Day describes the opposite experience in Desktop Dungeons. Its combat prediction shows damage you will take and pips for follow-up hits, but simulated events were not allowed to change game state, so effects like a Naga weakening you with each attack forced the team to duplicate state. Ideally a simulated event chain would take a game state and return a new one, repeating until one side died; a decoupled, copyable state would have made it easy. He adds that subtle displays, such as a missing second pip meaning you will die, make players think the game demands a lot of maths ([Danny Day 2018, 15:08](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=908)). If you want previews, make your game state copyable from the start.

### Signal the stakes ahead of the choice

Previews cover single actions. Signals cover situations. Darren Grey argues that games should signal danger clearly, by flashing the screen red, special threat messages, different wall colours on hard levels or highlighted bosses, to break the player out of a heroic-charge mindset; he also warns against monsters that look cuddly but are terrifying ([Darren Grey 2020, 20:21](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1221)). John Bond applies the same idea to route choice: door iconography, like Hades' room reward icons or a door's art and size, tells players what lies beyond so they can plan. Designers usually do not want to surprise players at these moments; even a forced choice like a big hellish portal should warn that it will be hellish ([John Bond 2024, 6:25](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=385)).

Feedback after the action has to register quickly too. Lisa Brown found original Rogue lacked intensity for her because its text-only combat made you watch your health to understand danger; in Nuclear Throne, Slay the Spire or Loot Rascals the outcome is visible at once ([Lisa Brown 2020, 11:23](https://youtu.be/BjqZdMW8U9Q?t=683)). Leif Bloomquist's most important change to his Commodore 64 roguelike since the previous year's demo, prompted by playtest feedback, went the other way: replacing sound-only combat feedback with explicit messages of damage dealt and misses ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 6:32](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=392)). The common point is speed of understanding, not a particular medium.

### Reminders on demand

The player should never have to memorise what the game can remind them of. Casey Yano calls Slay the Spire's hover tooltips his proudest feature; they once had a one-second delay, which was removed because waiting to recall what something did was more annoying than an instant tooltip ([Casey Yano 2022, 27:45](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1665)). Jim Shepard recommends presenting item function first and flavour text separately, as Magic cards and Tangledeep's item cards do, with stats in distinct colours and flavour underneath, so the text never obstructs players who do not care ([Jim Shepard 2018, 24:26](https://youtu.be/jd7K0EmkvPk?t=1466)).

Keep it on one screen where you can. Berman's advice for card combat is that it should all fit on one screen, as Slay the Spire's layout and most breakout mobile and strategy hits do ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 16:00](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=960)). Tarn Adams describes the same roguelike philosophy, avoiding separate shop screens and keeping everything on one screen where possible; Dwarf Fortress extends it to conversation, which happens as speech in the world so listeners can act while responding ([Zach Adams and Tarn Adams 2016, 24:56](https://youtu.be/Zh6dnx9FM1g?t=1496)). Digitisation can remove interface burdens entirely: Berman credits Hearthstone with turning Magic's turn-interrupting Counterspell into a hidden secret played on your own turn, keeping interaction while removing interrupts, and urges designers to embrace the constraints of digital play ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 14:02](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=842)).

### When displays mislead or overwhelm

Displays fail in recognisable ways:

- **Misread encodings.** Josh Grams subdivided each hex into four steps to show fractional velocity in his turn-based space flight prototype and drew a line of shadow markers ahead of the ship; many players read each shadow as one turn rather than the whole line as one turn ([Josh Grams 2020, 2:04](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=124)).
- **Accumulation.** Cat Manning notes that Crusader Kings II surfaces trait effects clearly through icons and tooltips, but long-lived characters pile up an overwhelming wall of icons that are hard to tell apart, and a stat like 60+ learning can only be traced by summing traits ([Cat Manning 2020, 15:19](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=919)).
- **Lost affordances in a reskin.** David Dunham reskinned Thousand Hells' cards as tiles. It is obvious how many cards remain in a deck but hard to tell how many tiles remain in a bag ([David Dunham 2026, 13:44](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=824)), though the horizontal tiles also gave more room for explanatory text with play unchanged ([David Dunham 2026, 15:37](https://youtu.be/oipNr8RE5bA?t=937)). A visual change can cost information the old form carried for free.
- **Walls of text.** Evan Debenham's fix for Shattered Pixel Dungeon's seven years of changes was a changelog presented as a grid of clickable icons, each opening the details for that item, character or enemy, so full detail fits a phone screen ([Evan Debenham 2021, 8:38](https://youtu.be/NMWQIdfCgQg?t=518)).

**In practice.**

- Preview anything that can be simulated, and build state you can copy so previews are cheap and exact ([Brian Cronin 2024, 27:04](https://youtu.be/jhcHlg7YhPg?t=1624)).
- Signal danger before the choice, not after ([Darren Grey 2020, 20:21](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=1221); [John Bond 2024, 6:25](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=385)).
- Make tooltips instant ([Casey Yano 2022, 27:45](https://youtu.be/KYlq0Msu6hc?t=1665)).
- Fit play on one screen where possible ([Benjamin Berman 2019, 16:00](https://youtu.be/DT9_7sW5knY?t=960)).
- Test whether players read your symbols the way you meant them ([Josh Grams 2020, 2:04](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=124)).

## What the interface says: messages, labels and tone

Every message, label and statistic tells the player something beyond its information: how to feel about an event, what the designer values, what the "real" way to play is. Decide what you want each one to say.

### The message log

The classic roguelike reports events in a text log, and not everyone thinks it should stay that way. Biskup's graphical Ultimate ADOM aims to show effects visually with very little text so players watch the environment instead of reading message boxes; text messages can be turned on, but the hovering texts in the latest ADOM showed him that watching is much more compelling ([Thomas Biskup 2018, 16:20](https://youtu.be/PTIsUSbQ0TA?t=980)).

Whatever style you choose must not cost information. Zack Johnson wanted Kingdom of Loathing's whole output convertible into haiku, but a game becomes unplayable if events are abstracted into jokes. Doing it properly meant categorising every kind of text the combat script could produce, writing haikus for each, and later putting exact numbers like HP lost into hover text ([Zack Johnson 2016, 10:28](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=628)). Even plain messages take work: Nicholas Feinberg notes that Crawl needs hundreds of lines of special-case code just to pluralise monster and item names correctly, because "add an s" fails for names like hippogriff ([Nicholas Feinberg 2020, 6:09](https://youtu.be/GMkBT4UbvAs?t=369)).

### Tone as design

Tone in the interface carries meaning. In Caves of Qud, Jason Grinblat's team kept the body swap feeling like a transgression by giving it no journal entry and no achievement, only a terse, neutral message: "your mind is stranded here". In a game full of baroque language, dropping to console-readout simplicity carried authorial weight ([Jason Grinblat 2021, 18:59](https://youtu.be/kvCky6BbTuE?t=1139)).

The interface can also be the character. Nathan Savant argues that UI exists to communicate character state, yet most games use it only for health; it can be animated, obscured or distorted to show mental state, such as blocking the screen for blindness or scrambling skills after a head blow ([Nathan Savant 2021, 9:06](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=546)). Andrea Interguglielmi's Nauticrawl makes the whole classic UI diegetic (part of the game world): the player sees only cockpit monitors, with hull integrity as HP, fuel as hunger and battery as stamina, and the map on a radar with fog of war ([Andrea Interguglielmi 2019, 4:07](https://youtu.be/wxmio1S3iN0?t=247)). Alexandra Leonhart reads the message log as an institution's feedback on your actions and sees an unexplored space in an unreliable message-log narrator ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:18:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=29902)). That idea runs straight into Johnson's rule, and the tension is worth noticing: a narrator that lies is a design choice only if the player can eventually tell.

### What labels say about how to play

How you present options states your view of them. Andrew Aversa lays out a scale for presenting permadeath: no option at all is the strongest statement of intent; a preselected toggle is a big nudge; nesting it in a submenu downplays it; hiding it behind file editing says you cannot do this; listing options with none highlighted is the most equitable and likely gets roughly even consideration ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 7:57](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=477)). Labels work the same way: Wolfenstein and Doom mock their easy modes, Celeste offers assists after a gentle screen recommending playing as intended first, and ADOM lists its modes equitably, though Aversa saw it later tell a standard-mode player they could progress to the "real" classic mode ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 9:50](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=590)).

Statistics are labels too, and some designers steer deliberately. Dan DiIorio refused Richard Garfield's suggestion of a win-rate statistic in Luck be a Landlord: a player who wins after four losses should feel triumphant, not be reminded of 20% ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 16:18](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=978)). Andrea Roberts's Roundguard puts unlocks, mastered relics and score progress front and centre each run, to say that dying did not erase what you learned ([Andrea Roberts 2020, 16:55](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1015)). NetHack's developers chose not to warn before a player breaks a conduct (a self-imposed restriction a player chooses to play under), because the point of a conduct is avoiding the actions that violate it ([Kawa 2019, 13:43](https://youtu.be/KLHJsJuJfYg?t=823)). And the game's last word on a run is itself an interface: Quinten Konyn describes DCSS's morgue file, a roughly 19 KB text record of a dead character covering overview, inventory, skills, spells, death messages, the map where you died, vanquished monsters, notes and timelines ([Quinten Konyn 2025, 2:07](https://youtu.be/a9flzzXJVcg?t=127)).

Aversa's equitable listing and DiIorio's or Roberts's deliberate steering are both legitimate. The difference is whether you have decided what message you are sending.

**In practice.** For each label, mode name and statistic, ask what it implies about the intended way to play, and whether you mean it ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 7:57](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=477)). Let style shape text but never hide game information ([Zack Johnson 2016, 10:28](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=628)).

## Windows onto the simulation: making deep systems legible

### Too many events, not too many commands

For simulation-heavy games the interface problem changes shape. Max Kreminski warns that games like Dwarf Fortress and Crusader Kings II expose complex simulations directly through inscrutable UI, leaving players lost in a deluge of mostly insignificant events. He does not want the simulation simplified, which would take creative burden off the player; he wants players given tools to make sense of it ([Max Kreminski 2019, 11:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=701)). Jasmine Otto calls such a tool a "narrative instrument": in a social simulation with hundreds of characters, the interface must let players aim their attention at the parts relevant to them, like a Sims player checking on a rival while 80 other Sims go unobserved ([Jasmine Otto 2021, 2:45](https://youtu.be/NjIDVIIg1lY?t=165)).

### Sense-making tools

The talks offer a set of concrete instruments:

- **A chronicle of the world.** Jonathan Lessard's game exposes its simulation through "chronicles", a live, exhaustive, hyperlinked wiki of the world inspired by Dwarf Fortress's Legends mode, which updates as the game advances and includes graphs such as population over time ([Jonathan Lessard 2023, 4:32](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=272)).
- **A journal that reorders fragments.** Caves of Qud logs each discovered history snippet about a sultan in chronological order, so fragments found out of order read as a story; before the journal, players had to take diligent notes ([Jason Grinblat 2017, 5:29](https://youtu.be/ClGAApZYIvI?t=329)).
- **Summaries of hidden state.** Manning describes how Crusader Kings III surfaces hidden AI personality as a two-word epithet built from the two most extreme of nine hidden attributes, so a compassionate but greedy character might show as a "vindictive ravener"; in CK2 the equivalent stats were unreadable without looking under the hood ([Cat Manning 2020, 19:11](https://youtu.be/q7E1N-fJnrA?t=1151)). Shepard suggests emoji, such as hearts, question marks and frowns, to show NPC relationship states cheaply and across dialects ([Jim Shepard 2019, 26:07](https://youtu.be/LKCRim02opc?t=1567)).
- **Abstraction.** Nic Tringali's The Banished Vault replaces orbiting bodies with a delta-v map, a tree of stable orbits with one or two energy numbers per hop, so a continuous physics problem becomes a readable graph ([Nic Tringali 2023, 3:02](https://youtu.be/nSJA2yVsTFM?t=182)).
- **Filters and search.** Mark R Johnson's Ultima Ratio Regum groups its roughly 500 dialogue questions by topic, filters them by NPC class, colours them by the player's fluency in the current dialect, and narrows them as you type ([Mark R Johnson 2019, 23:02](https://youtu.be/qh9vyoMviJI?t=1382)). Kreminski's Synthesifter, a designer-facing tool, pairs a filterable event log with positive and negative examples and live candidate matches for refining a pattern ([Max Kreminski 2020, 8:11](https://youtu.be/oaDI0lWkedg?t=491)).

### Show the seams

Aaron Reed argues that procedural text should usually show its seams, because players only appreciate variation once they can see what changed and why. In Ice-Bound nobody appreciated how text varied with the active symbols and emphasised themes until a mode was added that highlighted the varying text, which became a window into how their actions shaped the collaboration. He allows hiding procedurality when that is the intent ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 24:30](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1470)). The same holds for any hidden simulation: a change the player cannot see is a change they cannot value.

### Open problems

Two problems remain unsolved. Rich Wilson frames the lack of verbs for feelings like grief in first-person games as a problem of "interaction articulation": how players can express deeper intent, and whether the game has receptors for it. Radial menus give range but break immediacy; he sees VR hand interaction as a promising direction ([Rich Wilson 2021, 23:45](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1425)). Scott Anderson calls 3D or top-down falling-sand simulation a really hard interface problem: volumes are small because of memory and compute, and players struggle to see into them ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:41:11](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16871)).

**In practice.** Give players filters, histories and summaries of hidden state rather than a raw event feed ([Max Kreminski 2019, 11:41](https://youtu.be/BDcZSWHu8RQ?t=701); [Jonathan Lessard 2023, 4:32](https://youtu.be/D8A9dpITLAU?t=272)). Let them see what changed and why ([Aaron A. Reed 2020, 24:30](https://youtu.be/x0Xh4oCX9t0?t=1470)).

## Letters, tiles and symbols: choosing a visual vocabulary

The sections so far have been about what the interface shows and how the player drives it. The next two turn to the symbols themselves and the machinery that draws them. The argument over ASCII versus tiles is usually conducted as a matter of taste or nostalgia. The talks treat it more usefully, as a trade-off between what each kind of symbol makes easy and what it makes hard. Once you see the trade-off, the choice stops being about looks and becomes a question of what your player has to recognise, how fast, and how often ([Joel Ryan 2022, 13:57](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=837); [Evan Ovadia 2019, 4:36](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=276)).

### Association against differentiation

Joel Ryan, who drew the tileset for Sil-Q, gives the clearest frame, an idea he credits to an article he read. A visual vocabulary has to do two jobs: let the player *associate* a symbol with what it means, and let the player *differentiate* one symbol from another. ASCII is weak at the first and strong at the second. Every new roguelike asks you to learn a fresh set of glyph-to-monster mappings, but the letters of your own alphabet are about as easy to tell apart as symbols get, and a glyph classifies: a `T` tells you something about any troll-class monster before you have met it. Tiles are the reverse. You know a red dragon is a red dragon the moment you see it, but telling one tile from another at a glance is harder, so Ryan concludes that tile artists should spend their effort on differentiation ([Joel Ryan 2022, 13:57](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=837)).

Evan Ovadia states the cost side of ASCII bluntly. A newcomer looking at an ASCII screen sees noise: you cannot tell whether a `T` or a pair of quote marks is a friend, an enemy, an object or food, and you have to learn the code before the game becomes fun, whereas sprites are understood at a glance ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 4:36](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=276)).

> ASCII requires you to learn before you can have fun. — [Evan Ovadia 2019, 4:36](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=276)

But Ovadia also finds that, once learned, ASCII gives a clearer read of a tactical situation than detailed sprites: comparing identical scenes, he found the ASCII version easier to parse ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 7:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=425)). His own game, Domino, takes a middle path he calls symbolic graphics. A claw symbol does not say "goblin", but it does tell you that this is a scary enemy ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 4:36](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=276)). Domino's non-humanoid symbols let him emphasise each creature's distinguishing traits, and he deliberately leaves stairs, trees, tables and chairs off the domino-shaped backing tiles that creatures stand on, so threats stand out from scenery; he admits that the dominoes' height and the pentagonal terrain cost some clarity ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 7:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=425)). Symbols can also carry detail plain ASCII cannot, such as a small mark showing whether a character attacks with a sword or a gun, again at a slight cost in clarity ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 7:33](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=453)).

droqen pushes the abstraction argument from the design side. ASCII display and visible numbers boil a game's presentation down, so both developer and player can concentrate on the mechanics and what they say. In his Signal Pals, health drawn as three of five bubbles still makes the player think in numbers, and the frog and lizard enemies are purely iconic: one is simply the enemy with three hit points, the other the one with two ([droqen 2020, 6:41](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=401)). Darren Grey reads the genre's ASCII heritage the same way, as a priority of utilitarian gameplay over looks; it can be prettied up, as Brogue does, but the utility of the display matters more than its appearance ([Darren Grey 2020, 1:21](https://youtu.be/C2sm-z7Ag4U?t=81)).

### The imaginative case for letters

The second argument for glyphs is not about efficiency at all. The Rogue panel recalls ten or more players in the UC Santa Cruz stat lab screaming when a `T` appeared. The letter looked no scarier than a `B`, but after a while of play, Glenn Wichman says, you did not see a T on the screen, you saw a troll ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 9:01](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=541)). Leonard Richardson describes the same effect as a kind of imaginative play: the letter that is plain text at the top of the screen becomes a deadly monster on the map, and learning that `H` meant hobgoblin, or that the IBM PC's box-drawing characters were doorways, was the same pleasure as imagining his bedroom was a spaceship. He sets this against the school of thought that the `H` should be replaced with a realistic tile ([Leonard Richardson 2017, 4:41](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=281)).

Santiago Zapata points out that this was never planned. Rogue's terminal display relied on the player's imagination the way tabletop sessions did, but that was a happy accident: Rogue's developers have said they would have used graphics if they could ([Santiago Zapata 2018, 13:32](https://youtu.be/ZMdxP7fO6wE?t=812)). Nick Montfort sees a contribution in it anyway. Systems that make `@` and the letters A to Z stand for creatures defamiliarise the alphabet and suggest two levels of meaning at once, which he values even when the result is not visually spectacular ([Nick Montfort 2016, 22:40](https://youtu.be/blXH5pO8GA4?t=1360)).

### Encoding signals, and exploiting their limits

Whatever vocabulary you choose, it carries information beyond identity, and switching vocabularies means moving that information over deliberately. Ryan's work on Sil-Q is the worked example. Sil was not made with tiles in mind, and much of its state lived in brightness and tinting that tiles could not reproduce. Unaware monsters, drawn brighter in ASCII, got an exclamation mark; rage became swapped floor and wall tiles; weapons that glow blue near monsters they slay needed a three-layer system of floor, glow and weapon; damage numbers became overlay tiles ([Joel Ryan 2022, 8:56](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=536)). The rewards for doing this are real. Alan Malloy notes that DCSS ships both a character display and a tiles interface drawn by volunteer artists, because many people are unwilling to look at the ASCII version but would love to play the tiles one ([Alan Malloy 2017, 3:05](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=185)).

Ambiguity can also be a mechanic rather than a defect. In NetHack the Wizard of Yendor's decoys are drawn with the same purple `@`, so the limit of the character set creates real confusion about which symbol is the real wizard, as commentary on Adeon's speedrun points out ([Adeon 2017, 1:24:17](https://youtu.be/rIB0y_kwFuY?t=5057)). When ambiguity is not intended, give the player a cheap way to resolve it. Leif Bloomquist found players mistaking a low-resolution sign for a hammer in his Commodore 64 roguelike, so signs describe themselves when walked over ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 6:55](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=415)).

For tiles seen from above, Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt give readability rules from Sea of Rifts, where players must decode ship factions and types from afar. Put detail on the tops of objects, because that is what you see first; use strong colour and shape contrast, so spiky boats wear contrasting colours to signal danger and enemies are bright purple against the ocean; and exaggerate what matters, as with a weapon boom made unrealistically large so it reads at any camera distance ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 10:23](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=623)).

### Text as the graphics

A few designers push the vocabulary question to its limit and treat text itself as the display. Todd Furmanski proposes running a fully simulated 3D space while showing the player only a textual description with a simple examine parser, on the grounds that abstracting space is nothing new in a genre where a `D` is a dragon ([Todd Furmanski 2020, 10:58](https://youtu.be/ST6s_8ekeOg?t=658)). Elsewhere he pairs turn-based simulation with Myst-style static images: one composed picture per turn frees him from frame rates, characters stuck in walls and 16-button controller tutorials, and lets him spend his obsession on painterly styles such as pencil sketch or Mediterranean mosaic ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 30:50](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=1850)). Hardware can also take text away: making Dragon's Descent for the Atari 2600, Furmanski found that a text bitmap eats a sizeable chunk of the cartridge, so the game became an arcade action game and gave up what text does for roguelikes ([Todd Furmanski 2019, 5:37](https://youtu.be/l9eE4mT8xqI?t=337)).

The strangest example comes from print. Younès Rabii reads the novel *La Horde du Contrevent* as a roguelike that did not know it was one. It represents each character with a typographic symbol and lays them out on the page like a console display, so the reader sees the formation (a teardrop with the leader in front, for moving against the wind) and how tight the situation is, and it notates winds with punctuation: periods and commas for slowing wind, slashes for big gusts ([Younès Rabii 2022, 8:54](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=534)). Its pages are numbered downward from 700, turning the page count into a countdown towards a climax, much as a deeper dungeon level means you are nearer the end but at greater risk ([Younès Rabii 2022, 10:39](https://youtu.be/6ik6jB2YhZg?t=639)).

**In practice.** Choose your vocabulary for how quickly players must tell threats apart, not for how it looks in a screenshot. If you use tiles, put your effort into differentiation ([Joel Ryan 2022, 13:57](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=837)) and keep scenery visually quieter than creatures ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 7:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=425)). If you offer tiles alongside ASCII, list every signal the glyphs carried, such as brightness and tint, and re-encode each one ([Joel Ryan 2022, 8:56](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=536)). Where a symbol could be misread, make it explain itself on contact ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 6:55](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=415)).

## Building the display: terminals, fonts, grids and overlays

How you put characters and tiles on the screen shapes what you can show. The talks cover the full range, from 300-baud terminals to browsers, emoji and spreadsheets, and the constraints of each are specific enough to plan around.

### The terminal heritage

Rogue's interface was shaped by bandwidth. At 300 baud, 30 characters a second, with cursor addressing alone costing four characters, a full redraw was slow, so Ken Arnold drew the inventory as a small window in the upper-right corner and repainted only that region; he also cut keystrokes, such as the space presses needed after messages ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 12:08](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=728)). The screen size most terminal emulators still default to, 80 by 24 characters, comes from the DEC VT100, the de facto standard terminal of the late 1970s, as Tabitha Sable explains ([Tabitha Sable 2020, 11:45](https://youtu.be/6ohPU0sECFE?t=705)). Sable also explains why the curses library's optimisations were fragile: terminals interpret control sequences that alter their internal state, so on a mismatched terminal the first map might draw, but as soon as the character moves the optimised line redraw emits junk and the screen turns to line noise. She suggests reproducing it with a strict VT52 or VT100 emulator and `TERM` set to `vt220` ([Darren Grey et al. 2020, 48:50](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=2930)).

### Modern text-mode rendering

Patrick Devine's Go library for terminal sprites shows how simple the core loop can be: clear the screen, update sprite positions, redraw, forever. In his demo the main source of lag was the size of the terminal, and he relies on tmux to avoid actually performing full redraws ([Patrick Devine 2019, 3:14](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=194)). To get more resolution than one glyph per cell, he uses Unicode quadrant block characters: each cell has four independently lit "pixels", 16 combinations, drawn with the foreground and background colours. His character sprite is 6 by 6 cells, and because he has no drawing tool he authors sprites as ASCII text and converts them to quadrant characters ([Patrick Devine 2019, 6:39](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=399)). The caveats are practical. You need a good monospaced font and adjusted line spacing; Linux works best, while macOS and Windows terminals often break the spacing (he recommends iTerm2); and the code points involve UTF-16 handling rather than UTF-8 ([Patrick Devine 2019, 7:59](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=479)). Terminals offer 256 colours, more than 1980s 8-bit consoles, but each quadrant cell can show only two colours and its pixels are taller than wide, which causes artifacting ([Patrick Devine 2019, 10:05](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=605)).

Font geometry matters even when you are not using block characters. Gabriel Santos recommends a 1:1 font aspect ratio for top-down ASCII games and something nearer 1:2 for side or isometric views; after much experiment he settled on 16:29 for his side-view game ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 5:43](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=343)). To stay pixel perfect at any window size, he had more than 20 pixel-exact sizes of his font made, down to 3 by 5 pixels, and the game picks one dynamically as the window scales ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 6:42](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=402)).

Emoji grids bring their own trap. Joe Sondow notes that emoji are monospaced across platforms and so can form a grid, but no whitespace character matches their width, since ideographic and other spaces vary by platform; a perfectly aligned emoji grid therefore cannot use spaces. He turns this to advantage, using odd spaces to jitter his fish so they look more organic ([Joe Sondow 2017, 5:32](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=332)).

### Browsers and odd substrates

In the browser you can stop treating the UI as part of the game grid. Chris McCormick lays hit points and other text over the game canvas as ordinary HTML elements with a web font and absolute positioning, which makes UI iteration take seconds; rot.js can alternatively render fonts inside its console ([Chris McCormick 2021, 15:24](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=924)). For differing screen sizes he reads the character's position and centres the whole view on it with a CSS translate transform, and on mobile he simply shows less, smaller ([Chris McCormick 2021, 27:10](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1630)). In an engine, Sea of Rifts generates its parchment panels rather than drawing paper for every size: Birke's shader applies a paper texture and thresholds a noisy greyscale signed distance field (SDF) to get frayed pirate-map edges, nine-slicing makes resizing work, and screen-space noise plus per-element vertex colour offsets hide the repetition of a shared SDF; the same method produces shadows ([Alexander Birke and Sofie Kjær Schmidt 2025, 27:59](https://youtu.be/FC9GAL2piJI?t=1679)).

Unusual substrates show which display ideas are essential. Seth Cooper's Trogue, built in a tile rewrite language, implements exploration with two cover layers of large emoji: darkness, cleared permanently as you explore, and fog, which refills every move so only the area near the player is visible. Each move rewrites tiles near the player to clear both, and even the HUD must live on the grid, placed by dropping tiles and moving them into position ([Seth Cooper 2025, 10:51](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=651)).

> The fog refills every time the player moves but the darkness doesn't. — [Seth Cooper 2025, 10:51](https://youtu.be/K5FXzxDIQdQ?t=651)

Tyler Robertson shows that a spreadsheet works as a turn-based engine because it only updates when the player clicks: direction buttons drive X and Y values, and formulas across the grid draw an `@` wherever the coordinates match. The same property makes it poor for real-time games ([Tyler Robertson 2022, 8:23](https://youtu.be/hdhKErNIYgE?t=503)).

Input handling belongs with the display layer, because modes such as targeting change what a click on the grid means. Danny Day's Desktop Dungeons swaps the active click handler: casting a fireball removes the normal handler and installs a fireball handler listening to the same events, which emits a cast-fireball event on a grid click, or removes itself and restores the default on right-click or cancel. The default handler never needs to know how fireballs work, and new spells need no other system to know about them ([Danny Day 2018, 11:51](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=711)).

### Geometry and view

What the screen shows is also a choice about geometry. Zeno Rogue noticed that roguelike screenshots often show the whole level, which is rarer in other games, and uses HyperRogue's hyperbolic projections to combine a close view of the character with a large part of the level on one screen; players prefer different projections, so several are offered ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 27:02](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1622)). Lee Tusman's survey of one-dimensional dungeons finds the spare axis put to use: Stutterstep plays along a single line and shows items and equipment along the second dimension ([Lee Tusman 2020, 7:39](https://youtu.be/-e4gF_SKWPk?t=459)), and One Dimensional Dungeon can be played vertically, with a flip-flop mode that switches orientation every level ([Lee Tusman 2020, 9:31](https://youtu.be/-e4gF_SKWPk?t=571)). And not every display convention travels. Tyriq Plummer observes that line of sight, nearly universal in traditional roguelikes, is rare in roguelike platformers, which mostly use fog of war or darkness instead; he could not make line of sight run efficiently in real time in Catacomb Kids, which is now designed without it ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 18:28](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1108)).

**In practice.** Pick a rendering technique for the information it must carry: block characters buy resolution at the cost of two colours per cell ([Patrick Devine 2019, 10:05](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=605)), emoji grids cost you whitespace alignment ([Joe Sondow 2017, 5:32](https://youtu.be/4byHHDeVKoA?t=332)), HTML overlays buy fast iteration ([Chris McCormick 2021, 15:24](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=924)). Choose a font aspect ratio to suit your camera ([Gabriel Santos 2019, 5:43](https://youtu.be/5sFVVQcUWVE?t=343)). Keep input modes as swappable handlers rather than flags in one handler ([Danny Day 2018, 11:51](https://youtu.be/p48ArjJweSo?t=711)). Then test on the actual terminals, fonts, browsers and screen sizes your players will use, because these techniques depend on fonts, line spacing and terminal types ([Patrick Devine 2019, 7:59](https://youtu.be/ckDp6p4HbqA?t=479); [Darren Grey et al. 2020, 48:50](https://youtu.be/tmrYfnMrifw?t=2930)).

## Playing without seeing: blind and low-vision accessibility

Almost everything the talks say about blind players comes from one research project: Alexei Pepers' work on an accessible NetHack, presented in 2016 and revisited in a 2018 Q&A. That is a narrow base, and you should treat it as one team's well-tested findings rather than settled consensus. But it is detailed, it was tested with visually impaired players ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)), and its central claim, that roguelikes are unusually close to accessible already, should encourage anyone working in the genre ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 12:09](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=729)).

### The goal and the opportunity

Pepers starts from a gap. Accessibility research had focused on access more than on the games, producing titles that were fully accessible but simple and not very replayable; making Battleship accessible is easy but not much fun. Her project asked whether a deep, replayable game like NetHack could be made fully accessible ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 0:47](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=47)). Roguelikes turn out to be unusually good candidates. Because ASCII cannot show that you are levitating, the game tells you in text, and even graphical effects like a wand of lightning come with a text description; so much of the game is already text that relatively few changes make it fully accessible ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 12:09](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=729)).

The baseline is not good enough on its own, though. Some visually impaired players already play NetHack by having a screen reader read the raw map aloud as "hash dot dot dot hash", which Pepers calls terrible; they do it because they want to play that badly ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 2:15](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=135)). Combat text works fine; what blind players mainly struggle with is positional movement ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 25:36](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1536)).

### What the team built

The core addition was a view command that lists every visible object, monster and dungeon feature with its exact tile offset from the player, because in a tile-based game you need positions like "two tiles north" to interact with anything. A cursor-based "feel" mode lets the player probe individual tiles, and in hallways each move reports how many tiles are visible and accessible in each direction ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 5:34](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=334)).

Visually impaired players said the most taxing part of play was moving through the dungeon as a whole: holding a mental map of the level and backtracking through it. The team added a list of remembered features, such as staircases, altars and fountains, that the player can select to auto-travel to, and a way to select a visible item, walk over it and pick it up. The aim was to remove frustration without removing gameplay ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 7:18](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=438)). Pepers modelled these on DCSS's time-saving auto-path functions, and the NetHack dev team later implemented their own version of some of the changes ([Alexei Pepers 2018, 25:36](https://youtu.be/5y_IAdOwaYs?t=1536)).

### The unsolved problem: precise space in plain words

The hard problem is spatial. "You see a wand and a kobold to the southwest" does not tell you whether you can reach the wand first, whether you can route around the encounter, or whether you are lined up to zap. Interactive fiction sidesteps this by abstracting space into rooms; a tile roguelike cannot, and Pepers says giving precise positions in text that is neither technical nor verbose is really hard, and is where future work must go ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 16:24](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=984)). Every description sits between giving enough information to play and staying immersive without burying the player in text. The view command struck the balance ("you see your little dog named Sirius"); the hallway tile counts after every move did not ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 14:04](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=844)).

Each existing alternative solves part of the problem and costs something else:

- **Raw screen reading of the ASCII map** works and is miserable ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 2:15](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=135)).
- **Lists and auto-targeting.** Angband's monster list and auto-targeting make its combat accessible, but its map exploration cannot be done through text, so it suits players with partial vision who enlarge the tiles ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=280)).
- **Auto-explore.** Crawl's auto-explore lets blind players move through a level without seeing it, but they never know where they are and go from encounter to encounter, losing exploration ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=280)). This is the accessibility side of the automation argument in "Respecting the player's time" above: the same feature that removes a toll for one player removes the game for another. For games with irregular, Angband-style rooms, Pepers suggests offering auto-explore as an option for those who want it, paired with orientation aids such as absolute coordinates ("50 tiles right into the dungeon") rather than only local offsets ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 26:53](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1613)).
- **Dropping the map.** Fully accessible text and audio roguelikes, such as the audio game Entombed, get rid of the tile map and use interactive-fiction rooms instead. That changes the game fundamentally: combat becomes a choice of dodge or attack against the monster's choice, not positional tactics ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 3:06](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=186)).
- **Spatial audio.** Directional sound works for an accessible Doom, but in NetHack you need the exact tile, not a direction. Pepers thinks combining directional audio with precise text, to reduce text overload, is worth exploring ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 24:42](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1482)).

### Process lessons

The most transferable lesson is about testing. The team left the ASCII map on so screen readers could fall back on it; players immediately asked to turn it off, because the screen reader read the whole map after every useful line of text. Sighted developers misjudge how screen readers behave ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)).

> There's really no substitute for getting the feedback directly from visually impaired players. They know what's best for them. — [Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)

Real play also finds what designers did not imagine. NetHack players steal from shops by sending a pet in while standing in the doorway, which requires knowing exactly where the pet drops each item; the view command re-read the entire shop inventory each time. The team had not anticipated this, and Pepers suggests announcing where pets drop items as a fix ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 10:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=643)). Where players disagree strongly, such as compass directions against up/down/left/right, make it an option: any single choice angers half the user base, and options already fit the roguelike habit of configuration files ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 10:19](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=619)). And the work pays off beyond its audience. The view command helps newer players identify unfamiliar ASCII symbols and lets anyone learn in one keypress that the weapon across the room is a silver saber, an extra incentive to invest ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 13:15](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=795)).

### Later work

The ideas have spread. NetHack 3.6 added a listing of monster and object locations closely resembling the research team's, though buried in menus, and BrogueSpeak set out to make Brogue fully audio accessible without a screen reader by converting text to speech and sound internally ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 19:56](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1196)). Outside roguelikes proper, Chelsea Thompto's The Fog uses ARIA tags so screen readers skip its decorative generated symbol text and read only the legible words ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 7:20](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=440)). In browser roguelikes, Chris McCormick's HTML overlays can be reached by tab navigation; asked about it by an audience member, he saw a risk of players editing the game live, while the session host noted it could serve accessibility, and McCormick added that the game can be fully keyboard driven ([Chris McCormick 2021, 29:12](https://youtu.be/dJbUmDsyJRw?t=1752)). Andrew Doull singles out Roguelike Radio's episode on designing for visually impaired players, including how they use screen readers, as personally important to him ([Andrew Doull 2025, 8:16](https://youtu.be/NaqP13nkpfU?t=496)).

**In practice**, a feature list drawn from this work:

- A command that lists everything visible with exact offsets from the player ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 5:34](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=334)).
- A cursor that can probe individual tiles ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 5:34](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=334)).
- A list of remembered features with travel-to, and select-to-pick-up for visible items ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 7:18](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=438)).
- Optional auto-explore with an absolute position report ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 26:53](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1613)).
- An option to hide the map from screen readers ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)).
- Options for contested conventions such as direction words ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 10:19](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=619)).
- Decorative text marked so screen readers skip it ([Chelsea Thompto 2026, 7:20](https://youtu.be/-xrcmY7LNPI?t=440)).
- Testing with visually impaired players, early ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)).

## Testing for players unlike you: children, parents, newcomers and different minds

Pepers' central lesson, that sighted developers misjudge what blind players need ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 8:43](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=523)), generalises. Beyond vision, accessibility in the talks is mostly a testing discipline. You cannot design for players unlike you from first principles; you have to find cheap ways to simulate them, watch them, or listen for the signs that they are stuck.

### Listen for the recurring question

Caelyn Sandel gives the simplest diagnostic: questions and confusions that keep coming up among new players mark accessibility gaps in the interface or design. If newcomers repeatedly fail to find the same part of the UI, make it more apparent; work out how you are not speaking the new player's language, and speak it ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 21:11](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1271)). Her example of what not to do is Caves of Qud's F1 quick-start help, which offers "10 things you should do when you start to play" but is still technical reading that points to other menus. Many players will simply give up, and Sandel stresses that being daunted by it says nothing about whether they could master Qud's complexity ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 7:22](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=442)).

Tools face the same problem. JP LeBreton's Playscii opens on a pre-filled starting document instead of a blank page, which invites play immediately; it even has a bottom edge that invites panning, teaching that documents can be any size. Where the tool breaks conventions, a bundled manual covers the rest ([JP LeBreton 2019, 9:27](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=567)).

### Michael Langford's toolkit for children and parents

The most concrete material comes from Michael Langford, who designs for children playing with their parents. Almost every item is a test a small team can run without special equipment.

- **Hands.** Record a child playing with a variety of controllers. Kids climb up the controller and flick sticks fighting dead zones; during testing, remap shoulder buttons down and see whether they can then finish. Chorded held inputs almost always trip up children, and on keyboards they are an injury risk for adults too ([Michael Langford 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=331)).
- **Remapping.** In-game button remapping fixes almost all parents' control problems without reworking the scheme; system-level remapping is cumbersome and fails with multiple controllers. Hold-to-activate modes can become equippable items the player toggles to ([Michael Langford 2021, 6:16](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=376)).
- **Random input.** Kids snack, wiggle and bump every button. Test menus by shaking a wrapped controller at them, and add stronger confirmation wherever random presses could delete a profile, end a run or spend a rare item; pause and load menus are where the damage happens, and adults make the same accidents ([Michael Langford 2021, 9:29](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=569)).
- **Literacy.** Simulate a pre-literate player with a "fake localisation": replace your font's glyphs with unreadable characters of similar size.
