If someone else can still get through, a child probably can; where they cannot, add icons, such as a heart or a bullseye for archery, to the important text ([Michael Langford 2021, 10:24](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=624)).
- **Eyesight.** For parents' older eyes, play from one and a half times your normal distance from the screen, then cut and enlarge the on-screen text ([Michael Langford 2021, 10:58](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=658)).
- **Slow machines.** Run the game on slow hardware and look for deaths right after a load screen: players look away during the load and die on arrival. Langford cites Swords of Ditto as a problem case, and says not to optimise the loading, which is a lot of work, but to add a partially obscuring confirmation screen or a transit hub, which need not appear on fast systems ([Michael Langford 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=682)).

> Any time they die right after a load screen, that's what you got to fix. Don't go fix your load screen performance. — [Michael Langford 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=682)

Langford's co-op advice runs against a usual design instinct. Children survive multiplayer with simple "cheese" strategies such as circling and shooting, the kind a parent tells a child to use. Have testers role-play those deliberately weak strategies, note which items and characters enable them, and flip the incentive: fight cheese in single player, but let it work in multiplayer so the child can play alongside the parent ([Michael Langford 2021, 8:10](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=490)). Then check who those cheese-friendly characters are. Young children want to play a character like themselves, and although there is no ability difference by gender at those ages, a child will want the matching character if the easy ones do not offer it ([Michael Langford 2021, 8:32](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=512)).

### Different minds and different limits

Hannah Blair Salzman argues that roguelikes are especially valuable to neurodivergent players: they engage mind and hands without requiring hyperfocus on one enormous game of the kind that takes hundreds of hours, and she thanks roguelike developers for helping such players in ways they may not have imagined ([Hannah Blair Salzman 2022, 11:46](https://youtu.be/6GSXaM1PTMg?t=706)). This is a case for the genre's short, self-contained runs as an accessibility feature in its own right.

At the other end of the spectrum, accessibility can mean protecting players who want to be frightened. For immersive horror that blurs the line with reality, G blekkenhorst offered content warnings with a way to ask about specifics, an allergen list for touchable objects, and sealed real bones in The Archive, and recommends the tabletop-RPG practice of asking for lines and veils (topics to exclude entirely, and topics to keep off-screen) along with a list of content players do want. The goal is people "miserable in the exact way they want to be miserable" ([G blekkenhorst 2026, 27:50](https://youtu.be/uZdEXqRkBZA?t=1670)).

**In practice**, cheap tests a small team can run this week:

- Log every question new players ask; anything asked twice is a design bug ([Caelyn Sandel 2020, 21:11](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=1271)).
- Swap your font for gibberish glyphs and have someone play through ([Michael Langford 2021, 10:24](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=624)).
- Play from 1.5 times your usual distance ([Michael Langford 2021, 10:58](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=658)).
- Mash random buttons on every menu and see what you lose ([Michael Langford 2021, 9:29](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=569)).
- Run a build on your slowest machine and watch the moment after each load ([Michael Langford 2021, 11:22](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=682)).
- Check that every held or chorded input can be remapped or toggled ([Michael Langford 2021, 5:31](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=331); [Michael Langford 2021, 6:16](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=376)).
- Make your first screen something to play with, not a page of reading ([JP LeBreton 2019, 9:27](https://youtu.be/MJZvWgcxV0M?t=567); [Caelyn Sandel 2020, 7:22](https://youtu.be/NANqgqeqh2k?t=442)).

## Beyond the keyboard: platforms, controllers and the player's body

Roguelikes grew up on keyboards, and most talks assume one. A smaller group asks what happens when the input device, the screen or the network changes, and their findings suggest the change is not cosmetic.

### The controller is part of the game

Yong Zhen Zhou argues from alternative-controller ("alt.ctrl") design that redesigning a game's controller expands what the game is. Conventional design attends to what happens behind the screen; alt.ctrl design also designs the interface and sometimes the display. His hypothetical is a horror game wired to smart-home lights that switch off as a health bar, so the layout of your house, how fast you can run and whether someone else can help all become part of play ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 5:48](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=348)). Input semantics also set the player's role: pressing A to jump makes you Mario's puppeteer, while voice control would make you his drill sergeant ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 9:41](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=581)).

> If it was suddenly voice controlled, your role is like a drill sergeant. — [Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 9:41](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=581)

Zhou's view of physical input fits his caution, noted under automation above, that simplifying demanding inputs can strip a game's energy. It applies even when you never build a controller. Slay the Spire plays identically everywhere, but Zhou finds a hand full of Shivs feels better on a phone, because you physically fling the cards out; every input has a physical sensation that contributes to the experience ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 14:08](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=848)). His examples include Line Wobbler, a one-dimensional dungeon crawler played on a single LED strip and controlled by a spring door stopper because it wobbles nicely ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 3:35](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=215)).

### Adapting turn-based play to other inputs

Turn-based play changes what a controller needs to do, sometimes for the better. Josh Grams, making a turn-based space flight game, found that combining turning, accelerating and shooting in one turn was a UX problem: real time lets you do all three at once, but turns raise questions of how to specify and cancel parts of a move, and confirming each turn felt slow. One-step rotation took three turns to turn around, so he gave each direction its own key, and turning to any direction costs one turn ([Josh Grams 2020, 2:38](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=158)). On a gamepad, pointing the analog stick seemed perfect, but players rest their thumbs on the stick and small wiggles cost turns; merging consecutive aiming turns did not help enough. His cousin's suggestion fixed it: a single move button that accelerates when held and coasts when released, with an overlay showing where the stick points and when it will trigger a turn ([Josh Grams 2020, 6:50](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=410)).

The fact that a traditional roguelike waits for input makes surprising devices workable. Qristy Overton played Brogue on a custom Makey Makey dance pad. It works because Brogue needs only about 18 inputs (directions, search, rest, apply, inventory, throw, yes, no, enter) and turns advance only when a key is pressed. An off-the-shelf mat lacked enough buttons, and since every press needs one foot on a ground pad, the ground foil wore out; she would add more ground pads next time ([Qristy Overton 2021, 1:19](https://youtu.be/zlJNIJOog9M?t=79)). At the far end, Bad News is staged in a small room with a model theatre: the player uses an iPad and speaks commands from a printed sheet, such as knocking on a door, while a curtain opens whenever a live actor plays a townsperson from a hidden screen, and a "wizard" runs the simulation out of sight ([Bad News team 2016, 3:43](https://youtu.be/XFFyN10o87I?t=223)).

The player's environment counts too. Julian Jarboe asks sound designers to imagine their game on very different setups: a small ThinkPad with drugstore earbuds and no mouse on a cramped commuter train, a surround-sound system with a projector and recliner, a 4K monitor with good headphones in a rented bedroom. Designers already think about accessibility and numpads; this is "same deal but for ears" ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 5:15](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=315)).

### Reaching players wherever they are

Platform reach is itself an accessibility question: can the player get to the game at all? Alan Malloy describes DCSS's online servers, which let players play over SSH or in the browser through WebTiles from any device with an internet connection, with nothing to download. One game can be continued from home or work, updates arrive automatically, players can choose old versions that still receive severe bug fixes, and phone ports talk to the WebTiles server ([Alan Malloy 2017, 6:35](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=395)). Drew Streib's NAO server added a JavaScript terminal over websockets (Chromium's hterm) so people on networks that block telnet, such as at work, can play NetHack in a browser ([Drew Streib 2016, 18:16](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1096)). Thomas Biskup counts more than 24 platforms for ADOM, including Amiga and Raspberry Pi, maintained out of love even though few people play there, while requests for iOS and Android keep coming ([Thomas Biskup 2016, 23:17](https://youtu.be/a3ZYDA2JVSM?t=1397)).

Leif Bloomquist's Dungeon of the Rogue Daemon, presented across three talks from 2018 to 2020, takes cross-platform play furthest. A single shared server instance is played from a Commodore 64 client written in 6502 assembler, a JavaScript port for browser and mobile, and a telnet client, with a translation layer converting the view to PETSCII, ASCII or UTF-8 ([Leif Bloomquist 2018, 9:34](https://youtu.be/Y0K-e83wYnQ?t=574)). The JavaScript port exists because few people own an internet-connected C64; it keeps the original gameplay, controls, character set and sound effects, and the font binary is the only code the clients directly share ([Leif Bloomquist 2019, 4:16](https://youtu.be/ASGn5J9PHbs?t=256)). Shared play was a goal from the start, and Bloomquist's aim is that each client keeps the flavour of its platform while the game stays fair between them; the server is written in JavaScript, and by 2020 the mobile interface was still rough ([Leif Bloomquist 2020, 7:51](https://youtu.be/bpSnPNr6ETc?t=471)). His wider vision is that any retro machine, from a VIC-20 to an Apple II, could connect and play together ([Leif Bloomquist 2018, 9:34](https://youtu.be/Y0K-e83wYnQ?t=574)).

**In practice.** Design input around the gestures the platform does well, as with flinging cards on a phone, rather than porting keystrokes one for one ([Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 14:08](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=848)). When you map a turn-based game to analog or physical input, check that accidental input cannot spend a turn ([Josh Grams 2020, 6:50](https://youtu.be/TsaRxD3g_os?t=410)) and that the game still waits for a deliberate action ([Qristy Overton 2021, 1:19](https://youtu.be/zlJNIJOog9M?t=79)). Imagine the cheapest and the most lavish setup your game will run on ([Julian K. Jarboe 2020, 5:15](https://youtu.be/zGbQi5LJwIw?t=315)). And if you can let players reach the game from a browser or a remote server, you remove the barrier of installing it at all ([Alan Malloy 2017, 6:35](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=395); [Drew Streib 2016, 18:16](https://youtu.be/J4RK-3zW8vY?t=1096)).

## Tensions and open questions

### Automation against embodied effort

Ge's Cogmind, Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup and Angband automate repetitive actions with one right answer, and in DCSS the automation grew from players' own fixes ([Josh Ge 2016, 22:56](https://youtu.be/9se2M27LuOs?t=1376); [bhauth 2020, 3:43](https://youtu.be/tg-CjNodlmY?t=223); [Erik Osheim and Robert Au 2016, 13:27](https://youtu.be/eeSk665OXkM?t=807)). Against this, Zeno Rogue leaves auto-travel out of HyperRogue because navigation is the challenge ([Zeno Rogue 2025, 18:02](https://youtu.be/wOlSws-OI2o?t=1082)), Martin Pichlmair and Yong Zhen Zhou value physical execution as part of the experience ([Martin Pichlmair 2026, 30:10](https://youtu.be/EMb6B2cIJps?t=1810); [Yong Zhen Zhou 2024, 16:23](https://youtu.be/KRZHT-gktD0?t=983)), and Vagante makes menu time a risk on purpose ([Tyriq Plummer 2017, 23:46](https://youtu.be/OVSi3NzA0KM?t=1426)). Accessibility adds a third view. For blind players, Crawl's auto-explore is what lets them move through a level at all, but it also leaves them disoriented and strips out exploration; Pepers' answer is to offer it as an option and pair it with orientation aids ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 4:40](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=280); [Alexei Pepers 2016, 26:53](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1613)). The choice depends on whether the effort is the game you are making, and for whom: one player's toll is another player's skill, and a third player's only way in.

### Modernising against the people already fluent

Biskup calls power-user communities the biggest obstacle to mainstream interfaces ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 7:24](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=444)), yet he also promised ADOM's veterans no more overhauls that force them to unlearn what they know ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 6:51](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=411)), and Tabitha Sable shows how long familiar conventions survive once people are used to them ([Tabitha Sable 2020, 25:02](https://youtu.be/6ohPU0sECFE?t=1502)). His own route was to design Ultimate ADOM simple-first rather than reduce an already complex interface ([Thomas Biskup 2017, 27:09](https://youtu.be/iZUXjbcAfYs?t=1629)). For an existing game with an existing audience, the talks do not say how much relearning is acceptable.

### Fewer options against options as accommodation

Biskup argues that every visible option costs every player, and that good defaults beat long option pages ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 14:04](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=844)). The accessibility talks reach for options as the remedy: Pepers makes contested conventions, such as compass directions, configurable because any single choice angers half the users ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 10:19](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=619)), and Michael Langford finds in-game button remapping fixes almost all parents' control problems ([Michael Langford 2021, 6:16](https://youtu.be/wPN5bPxWXm8?t=376)). The two can coexist if accommodations sit in a structured menu where players expect them, as Ultimate ADOM's essentials-only options do ([Thomas Biskup 2019, 14:04](https://youtu.be/hnoF_bL-HjI?t=844)), but where the line falls is a judgement each game makes.

### Letters against pictures

Evan Ovadia says ASCII makes you learn before you can have fun ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 4:36](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=276)), and DCSS ships tiles because many people will not look at its ASCII version ([Alan Malloy 2017, 3:05](https://youtu.be/QV57CYrIZow?t=185)). Glenn Wichman, Leonard Richardson and droqen value glyphs for what the player's imagination and attention do with them ([Glenn Wichman et al. 2016, 9:01](https://youtu.be/IaB7iQhts_c?t=541); [Leonard Richardson 2017, 4:41](https://youtu.be/ntVjLNl2_ro?t=281); [droqen 2020, 6:41](https://youtu.be/6Whz8bvjAKo?t=401)), and Ovadia himself found a learned ASCII screen easier to parse than detailed sprites ([Evan Ovadia 2019, 7:05](https://youtu.be/Xwa1KbXqeGQ?t=425)). The association-differentiation frame Joel Ryan borrows turns the argument into a question of what your players must do most: recognise things on first sight, which favours tiles, or tell them apart quickly, which favours glyphs ([Joel Ryan 2022, 13:57](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=837)). Offering both, as DCSS does, keeps both audiences, but adding tiles means re-encoding every signal the glyphs carried, as Sil-Q's tileset had to ([Joel Ryan 2022, 8:56](https://youtu.be/UIsNv3UOzvA?t=536)).

### Speed against spectacle

Jeremiah Reid's rule is that animation must never block input ([Jeremiah Reid 2021, 11:16](https://youtu.be/xSYVQc7cH-4?t=676)); Thomas Robertson lets a rare super attack halt play as long as it can be skipped ([Thomas Robertson 2021, 4:00](https://youtu.be/f1t4yPjfZyM?t=240)); John Bond notes that polish makes players tolerate slow menus ([John Bond 2024, 9:04](https://youtu.be/bpGRyzWCWwk?t=544)). The reconciliation offered in this chapter is that ordinary moves never wait and rare spectacles may pause if the player can cut them short, but how rare is rare enough is left to the designer.

### Style against legibility

Kingdom of Loathing's haiku mode may restyle text but must not hide game information ([Zack Johnson 2016, 10:28](https://youtu.be/jNUMRG_tvrY?t=628)). Alexandra Leonhart sees an unexplored space in a message log that is an unreliable narrator ([Alexandra Leonhart 2026, 8:18:22](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=29902)), and Nathan Savant would obscure or distort the UI to show a character's mental state ([Nathan Savant 2021, 9:06](https://youtu.be/WTLPXhLjwLU?t=546)). Hiding or distorting information can be the point; nobody in the talks says how to do it without the player losing trust in the screen.

### Neutral presentation against deliberate steering

Andrew Aversa describes listing modes with none highlighted as the most equitable choice ([Andrew Aversa 2020, 7:57](https://youtu.be/kn2QkH5lByw?t=477)). Dan DiIorio and Andrea Roberts deliberately shape what players see about their own record, declining to show a win rate or putting unlocks front and centre ([Dan DiIorio 2025, 16:18](https://youtu.be/fSmaqjbU2xg?t=978); [Andrea Roberts 2020, 16:55](https://youtu.be/WtdCY6NxX6I?t=1015)). Both are legitimate; what matters is knowing which message you are sending.

### Unsolved problems

- **Precise space in plain words.** How to tell a blind player exactly where things are without technical or verbose text is, Pepers says, where future work must go ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 16:24](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=984); [Alexei Pepers 2016, 14:04](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=844)). Directional audio combined with text is one idea she thinks worth exploring ([Alexei Pepers 2016, 24:42](https://youtu.be/e8Itfp3MHQ4?t=1482)).
- **The clearest classic roguelike.** Justin Ma and Matthew Davis ask what a classic roguelike with the best, clearest UI would look like, and think it hard but worthwhile ([Justin Ma and Matthew Davis 2022, 19:56](https://youtu.be/rNi5nO5yqLs?t=1196)). Slashie asks how far the entry barrier can be lowered without losing the genre's essence ([slashie 2026, 9:07:12](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=32832)).
- **Expressing intent.** Rich Wilson's "interaction articulation", how a player expresses something like grief, has no settled answer ([Rich Wilson 2021, 23:45](https://youtu.be/wtlLa7BGZcs?t=1425)).
- **Seeing into volumes.** Scott Anderson calls the interface for 3D falling-sand simulation a really hard problem ([Scott Anderson 2026, 4:41:11](https://youtu.be/R8DSq8qSJ44?t=16871)).

## Checklist

1. What share of your schedule is set aside for UX, and does it start on day one?
2. Whose feedback shaped your interface: only veterans, or also people who have never played a roguelike?
3. Which actions are harder to operate than they need to be, as distinct from harder to win?
4. How many keys must a new player learn, and can every action be reached by mouse or touch?
5. Is movement your main verb, and which actions could be triggered by bumping or stepping instead of by a command?
6. Does every visible option earn its cost, and are detail levels built in rather than bolted on?
7. Can the player act as fast as they want, or does any animation or server round trip make them wait?
8. Which decisions have only one right answer, and have you automated them, optionally?
9. Which manual efforts are part of the fun, and which are tolls?
10. Can the player preview an action's outcome, and is your game state copyable so previews run the real code?
11. Are dangers signalled before the choice, and are tooltips instant?
12. What does each mode name, statistic and message tell the player about how they are meant to play?
13. If your game simulates a lot, what tools let the player find what matters and see what changed?
14. If you offer tiles and ASCII, has every signal of one been carried over to the other?
15. Have you tested with players unlike you: someone blind or low-vision, a child, someone who cannot read your font, someone on the slowest machine?
